newsitem.title: USA: Lawsuit filed against diet drug makers.
newsitem.headline: Lawsuit filed against diet drug makers.

text.p: Two law firms said they filed a class action lawsuit on Wednesday against makers of three popular prescription diet drugs, alleging that the companies failed to warn users about possible side effects.

The suit was filed a day after researchers at the Mayo Clinic announced that two of the diet drugs -- fenfluramine and phentermine -- may have been responsible for a thickening of the heart valves in at least 24 young women.
The two drugs were prescribed to 18 million people last year in a combination commonly called "fen-phen."

The lawsuit named as defendants several pharmaceutical companies that make or supply one or other of the diet drugs. The defendants include SmithKline Beecham Plc ; Abana Pharmaceuticals Inc.; and Ion Laboratories Inc., which all make phentermine.

Wyeth-Ayerst Laboratories Co., a division of American Home Products Corp, makes dexfenfluramine, another diet drug sold under the brand name Redux. It was also named as a defendant in the suit, which was filed in federal court in San Francisco, the San Francisco law firms of Arnold Laub and of Lieff, Cabraser, Heimann and Bernstein said.
Representatives of the companies could not immediately be reached for comment.
The lawsuit has two named plaintiffs but the lawyers asked a judge to certify the suit as a class action, filed on behalf of anyone in the United States who had taken one or all of the three drugs.
The suit said the U.S. Food and Drug Administration had approved fenfluramine, phentermine and dexfenfluramine for use separately, but had not approved the drugs for combination use.

It alleged that the manufacturers and distributors of the drugs failed to adequately warn doctors and consumers that the combination of drugs was not FDA-approved and had not been systematically tested in clinical trials.
It accused the companies of failing to give consumers proper warnings of possible side effects of the drugs.

The suit seeks unspecified compensatory and punitive damages. It also seeks medical monitoring to enable people who have taken the drugs to "monitor the existence of dangerous potential side effects caused by the drugs, including primary pulmonary hypertension and valvular heart disease."
A U.S. research team said last year that people taking diet pills made from fenfluramine or dexfenfluramine were six times more likely to develop high blood pressure in the lungs.
The named plaintiffs in the lawsuit are San Diego County, California resident Natalie Gardner and Edward Baker, who lives in Zephyr Cove, Nevada.

According to the lawsuit, Gardner suffered from hypertension resulting from the use of fenfluramine, phentermine and dexfenfluramine. The suit said Baker used dexfenfluramine prescribed to him, but it did not say if he had suffered any ill effects.
